chunks: "Bus contention is when two or more drivers try to drive the same wire at the same time with different values: one is pulling it high and another is pulling it low.
With push-pull outputs that's a direct path from supply to ground through the two output stages, limited only by their on-resistances.
Quick numbers: two pins each with about 25 ohms of on-resistance fighting on a 3. 3 volt line. The current is 3.
3 over 50, about 66 milliamps, and the wire sits around half the supply, 1. 65 volts, which is neither a valid high nor a valid low.

That's bad on three counts: the receivers read garbage, the pins are probably beyond their current rating, and the heat, roughly 100 milliwatts in each output transistor, can damage or at least age the parts.

It happens when two masters drive a shared line, when software sets two pins as outputs at once, when a device fails to release the bus, and dynamically on a bidirectional bus when one driver turns on before the other has fully turned off.
To prevent it: only one driver at a time, enforced by design.

Use tri-state drivers with enable control and a dead time between turning one off and the next on; use open-drain outputs with a pull-up for shared lines, like I2C; use chip selects so only one slave drives MISO; add series resistors to limit the fault current; and in firmware make sure pins come up as inputs at reset."
